Choose a pairing that fits the home

Hybrid heating combines equipment and a control strategy

Gas furnace

The gas furnace takes over at the selected changeover. Its blower also moves air through the indoor coil during heat pump operation. Blower capacity and furnace condition decide whether an existing unit fits the pairing.

Heat pump

The outdoor heat pump moves heat into the home and provides summer cooling. Cold-weather output determines how much heating the furnace supplies. Compare model-specific performance on the heat pumps page.

Thermostat

Dual-fuel compatibility lets the thermostat coordinate gas heat and heat pump operation. An outdoor temperature sensor or supported temperature input informs changeover. Wiring, source lockout, and staging must match the equipment instructions.

Evaporator coil

The indoor evaporator coil transfers heat between refrigerant and the home’s air. A match requires the specified outdoor unit, refrigerant compatibility, and adequate airflow. Coil dimensions and connections also determine installation work.

American Standard furnace

City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment. A replacement furnace must support the heat pump’s airflow and control requirements. Comparing both components together identifies the blower capacity and connections needed for a compatible pairing.

Outdoor unit and line set

Manufacturer clearances preserve airflow and service access around the outdoor unit. Chicago gangways and roof locations affect placement and equipment access. Refrigerant line length, routing, and insulation connect that location to the indoor coil.

Hybrid heating questions for Chicago homes

How does a dual-fuel system choose between the heat pump and the gas furnace in winter?

A hybrid system runs two heat sources from one thermostat. The heat pump carries the house in mild weather, moving heat from outdoor air into the ducts. Once the outdoor temperature falls past a set changeover point, the control hands the house to the gas furnace and the heat pump stops. In most Chicago setups only one source runs at a time, so the burner is never fighting the compressor. That handover is set at installation, and both modes should be proved before the crew leaves. From inside the house the change shows up only as a short pause in airflow.

What is the balance point, and how is it set for a Chicago home?

Two balance points matter. The thermal balance point is the outdoor temperature where heat pump output stops covering the home's heat loss. The economic balance point is where gas becomes the cheaper way to heat. Insulation, window area, duct condition and equipment capacity move the thermal figure. Utility rates move the economic one, so neither is fixed for every Chicago block. The changeover setting on the thermostat is normally placed at whichever of the two arrives first. A setting chosen carelessly is the most common reason a hybrid install disappoints, because the furnace takes over earlier than the design assumed.

How cold can the heat pump keep heating before the furnace takes over?

A standard air-source heat pump on a Chicago install is usually handed over to the furnace somewhere between 25 and 35 degrees. A cold-climate model holds useful output much lower, and changeover settings of 5 to 15 degrees are common on those systems. The band is wide because heat pump capacity falls as the outdoor temperature falls, while the heat loss of the house rises at the same time. Where those two lines cross depends on the insulation of the building and the capacity the outdoor unit was sized for. Equipment performance data sets that number for a given house, not a rule of thumb.

Does hybrid heating actually lower a Chicago heating bill?

Sometimes, and the arithmetic is honest either way. Heat pump heating is cheapest in the shoulder seasons, when outdoor temperatures sit well above the changeover point. Gas rates measured against electric rates decide where the economic crossover falls, and those rates move. Savings then depend on how many heating hours of a Chicago winter sit above that crossover. The case where hybrid does not pay is a house with cheap gas service and a sound, efficient furnace, since the furnace already covers the cold hours at low cost. City & Suburban quotes upfront and puts the exact price in writing, with no hidden fees, so equipment cost stays separate from projected savings.

Can a heat pump be added to a gas furnace that still has years left in it?

Often, yes, and that is the least expensive route into hybrid heating. A sound gas furnace stays, a heat pump goes in outdoors, and a matched coil sits in the supply plenum. The furnace blower then serves both heat sources. Furnace age, heat exchanger condition, blower capability and the electrical panel all have to be checked before equipment is selected. A furnace near the end of its life makes a poor partner for new outdoor equipment. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment and repairs all makes and models, so a furnace from another brand is no barrier. Where the furnace is already failing, replacing both at once usually costs less than two separate projects.

Which Chicago homes suit a hybrid setup, and which homes do not?

The strong candidate is a ducted house with a gas furnace that is due for replacement. A house already replacing the air conditioner also qualifies, because one outdoor unit then cools in summer and heats through the shoulder seasons. Homes heated by steam or hot water without ducts are not candidates until a duct system exists, which is a different project altogether. An undersized electrical service, no outdoor space for the unit, or a cracked heat exchanger has to be settled first. An estimate for dual fuel should name which of those applies before equipment is ordered, not after.

Which thermostat and wiring does hybrid heating need?

Dual-fuel needs a thermostat that knows which heat source is active. It also has to lock the heat pump out below the changeover temperature, which a plain furnace thermostat cannot do. The job needs outdoor temperature sensing, a common wire, and in most homes a dedicated circuit and an outdoor disconnect. Old two-wire thermostat cable in a bungalow or greystone usually has to be replaced on the same visit. Lockout and auxiliary heat staging are set once the control is wired. The system should then run in heat pump mode and in furnace mode, so the logic is proved before the crew leaves.

Do the ducts need work before a heat pump runs alongside the furnace?

Sometimes, and it is worth knowing before the equipment is ordered. A heat pump delivers air at a lower temperature than a gas furnace. It therefore has to move more air to keep the same rooms comfortable. A duct system sized tightly around a furnace alone can turn drafty or noisy once the heat pump takes over. Return air is the usual bottleneck in bungalows and two-flats, where one central return serves a whole floor. Static pressure and return capacity belong in the estimate, so any duct changes are named and priced before install day. Selling equipment the ducts cannot feed only moves the complaint from the furnace to the heat pump.

What happens during the estimate visit, and what should a homeowner ask before accepting a dual-fuel proposal?

The visit should start with the building, not an equipment list. An estimate for dual fuel should measure existing furnace capacity and check duct size, return air, the electrical panel and the outdoor space. Five questions then separate a real proposal from a brochure. Which heat pump and furnace are paired, and what changeover temperature is set. Who tests both modes, whether duct and electrical work are priced separately, and who handles the permit. Options should name the tradeoffs, including staying with a furnace alone where hybrid does not pay. City & Suburban quotes upfront and puts the exact price in writing before any work begins, with no hidden fees.

What decides the price of a hybrid heating installation?

Scope decides it, not a list rate. The movers are whether the furnace is replaced or kept, and the capacity of the outdoor unit. The coil and line set, electrical work, and any changes to ducts or venting count too. Access matters as well, since a condo, a walk-up or a roof location is harder to work in. A two-day schedule is common when furnace, coil, outdoor unit and thermostat all change together. Disposal and permit fees add to the total. City & Suburban quotes upfront and puts the exact price in writing before work starts, with no hidden fees. Financing through Wells Fargo Home Projects is available, subject to credit approval.

Are there rebates or credits for adding a heat pump in Chicago?

Programs exist and change often, so each one is worth checking before equipment is ordered. The federal efficiency tax credit applies to qualifying high-efficiency heat pumps and furnaces. ComEd runs residential electric efficiency programs and Nicor Gas runs residential gas efficiency programs, each with its own equipment requirements. Eligibility turns on the rated efficiency of the exact models installed, which is why a proposal has to name the pairing. Which programs apply is confirmed at the estimate against the equipment selected. City & Suburban quotes upfront with no hidden fees, so any credit or rebate stays separate from the installed price.

Does a dual-fuel conversion need a City of Chicago permit?

Replacing heating equipment in the city is permitted work. A City of Chicago permit covers the equipment change, and the electrical work a heat pump adds normally sits in the same filing. Permit records for the 24 months to August 2026 show furnace and heat pump replacements filed routinely, so this is ordinary rather than exceptional. The practical questions are who files it, how much time the filing adds, and whether the fee sits inside the quote. Equipment replacements in Chicago generally need a City permit, and the written quote should say who pulls it. A permit also leaves a record of the work for a future sale or appraisal.

Is a hybrid system safe to run through a Chicago deep freeze?

The gas half carries the same obligations as any furnace: clean combustion, sound venting and an intact heat exchanger. Illinois requires carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning equipment under the Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act. That applies to a hybrid install exactly as it does to a furnace. The failure specific to dual-fuel is quieter. If the changeover never fires, the heat pump keeps running below the temperature it can serve and the house drifts cold. A heating service on a dual-fuel system should cover combustion, flame sensing and the switchover logic. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, so both halves of a mixed-brand pairing can be serviced.

What counts as an emergency, and how quickly can a technician get there?

The symptom decides. Air from the vents feels cooler on heat pump heat than on gas heat, which is normal. A short cool stretch near freezing is usually a defrost cycle. No heat in a hard freeze is a same-night call. So is a burning smell, a breaker tripping on the outdoor unit, or a furnace locking out on repeated ignition attempts. City & Suburban runs emergency HVAC service every day till midnight, except Sundays. Same-day service is offered when the schedule allows, across 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs. Maintenance plan members get priority dispatch when a cold snap fills the board.

Does hybrid heating keep a Chicago rental unit within the Heat Ordinance?

Where the landlord supplies the heat, the Heat Ordinance sets minimum indoor temperatures from September 15 to June 1. The rule is at least 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. each day. The overnight minimum is 66 degrees, from 10:30 p.m. to 8:30 a.m. (Chicago Municipal Code 13-196-410). The code lists exceptions, so it stands as the general rule. A dual-fuel system meets that standard the way a furnace does, because the gas side carries the coldest hours. The changeover setting is what matters, since a heat pump asked to work below its range falls behind. On a rental building that setting should be chosen with the ordinance duty in mind.

How much maintenance does a dual-fuel system need, and who services both halves?

Two heat sources mean two seasonal services, not one. The gas furnace needs burner, flame sensor, condensate and venting checks before winter. The heat pump needs refrigerant charge, coil cleaning and defrost checks, and it now works in both seasons rather than only summer. A weak charge is easy to miss and shows up as a higher winter bill, because the system drops onto the furnace earlier than planned. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, so one company can cover a furnace and a heat pump of different brands. Maintenance plans add seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch and member discounts for homes running two systems.

sections.html:
Hybrid heating questions for Chicago homes

How does a dual-fuel system choose between the heat pump and the gas furnace in winter?

A hybrid system runs two heat sources from one thermostat. The heat pump carries the house in mild weather, moving heat from outdoor air into the ducts. Once the outdoor temperature falls past a set changeover point, the control hands the house to the gas furnace and the heat pump stops. In most Chicago setups only one source runs at a time, so the burner is never fighting the compressor. That handover is set at installation, and both modes should be proved before the crew leaves. From inside the house the change shows up only as a short pause in airflow.

What is the balance point, and how is it set for a Chicago home?

Two balance points matter. The thermal balance point is the outdoor temperature where heat pump output stops covering the home's heat loss. The economic balance point is where gas becomes the cheaper way to heat. Insulation, window area, duct condition and equipment capacity move the thermal figure. Utility rates move the economic one, so neither is fixed for every Chicago block. The changeover setting on the thermostat is normally placed at whichever of the two arrives first. A setting chosen carelessly is the most common reason a hybrid install disappoints, because the furnace takes over earlier than the design assumed.

How cold can the heat pump keep heating before the furnace takes over?

A standard air-source heat pump on a Chicago install is usually handed over to the furnace somewhere between 25 and 35 degrees. A cold-climate model holds useful output much lower, and changeover settings of 5 to 15 degrees are common on those systems. The band is wide because heat pump capacity falls as the outdoor temperature falls, while the heat loss of the house rises at the same time. Where those two lines cross depends on the insulation of the building and the capacity the outdoor unit was sized for. Equipment performance data sets that number for a given house, not a rule of thumb.

Does hybrid heating actually lower a Chicago heating bill?

Sometimes, and the arithmetic is honest either way. Heat pump heating is cheapest in the shoulder seasons, when outdoor temperatures sit well above the changeover point. Gas rates measured against electric rates decide where the economic crossover falls, and those rates move. Savings then depend on how many heating hours of a Chicago winter sit above that crossover. The case where hybrid does not pay is a house with cheap gas service and a sound, efficient furnace, since the furnace already covers the cold hours at low cost. City & Suburban quotes upfront and puts the exact price in writing, with no hidden fees, so equipment cost stays separate from projected savings.

Can a heat pump be added to a gas furnace that still has years left in it?

Often, yes, and that is the least expensive route into hybrid heating. A sound gas furnace stays, a heat pump goes in outdoors, and a matched coil sits in the supply plenum. The furnace blower then serves both heat sources. Furnace age, heat exchanger condition, blower capability and the electrical panel all have to be checked before equipment is selected. A furnace near the end of its life makes a poor partner for new outdoor equipment. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment and repairs all makes and models, so a furnace from another brand is no barrier. Where the furnace is already failing, replacing both at once usually costs less than two separate projects.

Which Chicago homes suit a hybrid setup, and which homes do not?

The strong candidate is a ducted house with a gas furnace that is due for replacement. A house already replacing the air conditioner also qualifies, because one outdoor unit then cools in summer and heats through the shoulder seasons. Homes heated by steam or hot water without ducts are not candidates until a duct system exists, which is a different project altogether. An undersized electrical service, no outdoor space for the unit, or a cracked heat exchanger has to be settled first. An estimate for dual fuel should name which of those applies before equipment is ordered, not after.

Which thermostat and wiring does hybrid heating need?

Dual-fuel needs a thermostat that knows which heat source is active. It also has to lock the heat pump out below the changeover temperature, which a plain furnace thermostat cannot do. The job needs outdoor temperature sensing, a common wire, and in most homes a dedicated circuit and an outdoor disconnect. Old two-wire thermostat cable in a bungalow or greystone usually has to be replaced on the same visit. Lockout and auxiliary heat staging are set once the control is wired. The system should then run in heat pump mode and in furnace mode, so the logic is proved before the crew leaves.

Do the ducts need work before a heat pump runs alongside the furnace?

Sometimes, and it is worth knowing before the equipment is ordered. A heat pump delivers air at a lower temperature than a gas furnace. It therefore has to move more air to keep the same rooms comfortable. A duct system sized tightly around a furnace alone can turn drafty or noisy once the heat pump takes over. Return air is the usual bottleneck in bungalows and two-flats, where one central return serves a whole floor. Static pressure and return capacity belong in the estimate, so any duct changes are named and priced before install day. The visit should start with the building, not an equipment list. An estimate for dual fuel should measure existing furnace capacity and check duct size, return air, the electrical panel and the outdoor space. Five questions then separate a real proposal from a brochure. Which heat pump and furnace are paired, and what changeover temperature is set. Who tests both modes, whether duct and electrical work are priced separately, and who handles the permit. Options should name the tradeoffs, including staying with a furnace alone where hybrid does not pay. What decides the price of a hybrid heating installation?

Scope decides it, not a list rate. The movers are whether the furnace is replaced or kept, and the capacity of the outdoor unit. The coil and line set, electrical work, and any changes to ducts or venting count too. Access matters as well, since a condo, a walk-up or a roof location is harder to work in. Are there rebates or credits for adding a heat pump in Chicago?

Programs exist and change often, so each one is worth checking before equipment is ordered. The federal efficiency tax credit applies to qualifying high-efficiency heat pumps and furnaces. ComEd runs residential electric efficiency programs and Nicor Gas runs residential gas efficiency programs, each with its own equipment requirements. Eligibility turns on the rated efficiency of the exact models installed, which is why a proposal has to name the pairing. Which programs apply is confirmed at the estimate against the equipment selected. City & Suburban quotes upfront with no hidden fees, so any credit or rebate stays separate from the installed price.

Does a dual-fuel conversion need a City of Chicago permit?

Replacing heating equipment in the city is permitted work. A City of Chicago permit covers the equipment change, and the electrical work a heat pump adds normally sits in the same filing. Permit records for the 24 months to August 2026 show furnace and heat pump replacements filed routinely, so this is ordinary rather than exceptional. The practical questions are who files it, how much time the filing adds, and whether the fee sits inside the quote. Equipment replacements in Chicago generally need a City permit, and the written quote should say who pulls it. A permit also leaves a record of the work for a future sale or appraisal.

Is a hybrid system safe to run through a Chicago deep freeze?

The gas half carries the same obligations as any furnace: clean combustion, sound venting and an intact heat exchanger. Illinois requires carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning equipment under the Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act. That applies to a hybrid install exactly as it does to a furnace. What counts as an emergency, and how quickly can a technician get there?

The symptom decides. Air from the vents feels cooler on heat pump heat than on gas heat, which is normal. A short cool stretch near freezing is usually a defrost cycle. Does hybrid heating keep a Chicago rental unit within the Heat Ordinance?

Two heat sources mean two seasonal services, not one. The gas furnace needs burner, flame sensor, condensate and venting checks before winter.
